# The Architecture Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

![](images/ch01-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="Compact Lighthouse intent expands into a cross-stack specification, an AI-native design system, checked evidence, and a separate commitment decision."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers."
>
> — Richard Hamming, *Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* (1962) [@Hamming1962NumericalMethods]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Richard Hamming, a Turing Award–winning mathematician and computer scientist, argued that computing should yield insight rather than raw data. The distinction is central to this chapter. An AI-native design system should help architects ask better questions, explain hardware mechanisms, and defend decisions; it should not merely generate candidate designs faster.
:::

Computer architecture expands what can be built not by accelerating isolated drafting tasks, but by co-evolving design methodologies alongside physical silicon constraints. Historically, lasting transitions never merely sped up manual drawing. Instead, they introduced higher-level abstractions, automated synthesis paths, and rigorous verification harnesses that systematically exposed flawed assumptions before committing millions of dollars to physical mask sets. That history frames the central challenge for AI-native system design: while generative models can propose candidate microarchitectures in seconds, real silicon must close setup and hold timing across process corners, dissipate heat through passive packaging, and run deep software stacks without functional deadlocks or security vulnerabilities. A syntax-clean register-transfer level (RTL) netlist that misses timing by 150\ ps or leaks unbudgeted milliwatts is not an architectural near-miss; it is scrap silicon.

An architecture moonshot therefore demands a closed-loop design system: a workflow that carries compact system intent through multi-level compilers, cycle-accurate simulation, and formal signoff checks to a defensible architectural recommendation. The compute overhead, tooling complexity, and verification burden of learned methods are justified only when the complete design system improves the architectural outcome, reduces non-recurring engineering cost, or achieves both. Testing whether learned capabilities transform architectural practice rather than merely accelerating local drafting requires an industrial-grade engineering challenge: one that couples workloads, compiler stacks, microarchitectures, and physical silicon signoff under strict real-world constraints.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
This chapter establishes the following learning objectives:

- **Define** the three operational layers of AI in architecture (point-task assistance, subsystem optimization, and cross-boundary system design) and the Architecture 2.0 moonshot.
- **Decompose** compact system intent into explicit cross-stack architecture requirements.
- **Distinguish** generated artifacts from verifiable architecture results.
- **Evaluate** the architecture result separately from the incremental contribution of the design system.
- **Separate** the technical evaluation result from the commitment decision a named human authority owns.
:::

## Historical Context and Design Transitions

Every major era in computer architecture has advanced by redefining the boundary between human intent and automated tool execution. When transistor counts outpaced manual drafting in the late 1970s, layout designers initially attempted to scale polygon drafting by expanding engineering headcount. That brute-force scaling collapsed under geometric complexity and interconnect density. The Mead–Conway very-large-scale integration (VLSI) methodology resolved this crisis not by speeding up manual polygon drawing, but by introducing structured design rules and scalable abstractions that decoupled logical architecture from foundry-specific lithography [@MeadConway1980VLSI].[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] When reduced-instruction-set computing (RISC) arrived, it replaced intuitive, microcode-heavy instruction set expansion with a quantitative, benchmark-driven contract linking compiler behavior directly to hardware execution cost [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC].

Later, logic synthesis succeeded not because it generated gates faster, but because formal equivalence checkers (such as Synopsys Formality [@Formality]) and static timing analysis (STA) allowed downstream tools to mathematically prove correctness and reject invalid gate-level implementations before committing capital to masks [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Veripool2026Verilator]. In each era, an idea became consequential because engineering teams could systematically apply, inspect, and improve the methodology built around it. While each transformation relied on different technical mechanisms, every established design methodology pairs an input abstraction with an expanded design object and a dependable verification harness (@fig-design-method-progression).

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

![**Design method advances expand system expressiveness and verification depth.** Historical design advances (from Mead–Conway VLSI design rules [@MeadConway1980VLSI] and the RISC hardware–software contract [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC] to register-transfer level (RTL) logic synthesis [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization] and parameterized generators) each connect an input abstraction to a larger design object and dependable verification infrastructure. AI-native system design appears separately as a prospective methodology that carries compact intent and live project state through existing simulators and electronic design automation (EDA) checks to a supported comparison, without displacing authoritative signoff tools.](images/fig-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="100%" fig-alt="Historical progression through Mead–Conway design rules and abstractions, the RISC hardware–software contract, RTL logic synthesis, and reusable hardware generators. Each established method connects an input abstraction to a design object and a dependable check or infrastructure. A separate prospective case shows an AI-native design system connecting system intent and current project state through existing tools and checks to a supported comparison or finding with stated alternatives and limits; the result may reject a candidate or retain the reference design."}

AI-native system design enters this progression as a prospective methodology rather than an established tier. It tests whether compact system intent and live project state can reach a supported architecture result through existing simulators and electronic design automation (EDA) toolchains. Rather than displacing established verification infrastructure, an AI-native methodology proves its value only when generated outputs withstand those same authoritative physical and formal checks.

## Architecture 2.0 Principles

The natural software-engineering impulse is to treat hardware generation as just another sequence prediction task. That intuition collapses in physical silicon. In software, generative models train on vast public corpora ($2{,}583.86\ \text{GB}$ across Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, and Rust in *The Stack v2*) backed by package ecosystems with millions of modular libraries (@fig-ch01-money-plot-data-gap-funnel, Panel a). In contrast, public hardware description code across all hardware description languages (HDLs) combined totals barely $3.76\ \text{GB}$: a $687\times$ data volume deficit. Worse, raw public HDL files undergo severe physical synthesizability attrition (@fig-ch01-money-plot-data-gap-funnel, Panel b): of nearly 189,000 public hardware repositories, fewer than 1% contain enough build harness to elaborate in EDA tools, and only 160 designs ($<0.1\%$) represent complete, design rule checking (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS) clean tapeout silicon [@LozhkovEtAl2024TheStackV2; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet; @VerilogEval]. A model trained on open GitHub repositories learns toy modules and syntax fragments rather than tapeout-clean physical designs. Generative models can emit syntax faster than engineering teams can evaluate it,[^fn-foundation-model-c01] widening the scissors gap between candidate generation velocity and physical signoff throughput (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales). Producing alternatives faster helps only when the design workflow can qualify what those alternatives mean physically.

![**The software versus hardware training data volume gap and synthesizability funnel.** Panel (a) compares deduplicated public source code volume in The Stack v2 across major software languages ($2{,}583.86\ \text{GB}$ across Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, and Rust) against all hardware description languages combined ($3.76\ \text{GB}$ across Verilog, SystemVerilog, and VHDL), exposing a $687\times$ raw data deficit alongside a $5{,}945\times$ package registry disparity ($3.9\text{M}$ software packages vs. $656$ open silicon cores) [@LozhkovEtAl2024TheStackV2]. Panel (b) traces the steep $1{,}180\times$ physical synthesizability attrition funnel across $189{,}000$ public HDL repositories: only $37{,}800$ form complete multi-file project graphs, $1{,}890$ contain executable testbenches, $420$ pass logic synthesis, and exactly $160$ achieve clean DRC and LVS signoff for manufacturing [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet; @VerilogEval].](images/fig-ch01-money-plot-data-gap-funnel){#fig-ch01-money-plot-data-gap-funnel width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel visualization of the software versus hardware training data gap. Panel A shows a bar chart comparing 2,583 GB of software source code against 3.76 GB of HDL code, illustrating a 687x volume deficit. Panel B shows a funnel diagram tracing 189,000 public hardware repositories down to 160 clean DRC and LVS tapeout-grade designs."}

[^fn-foundation-model-c01]: **Foundation model**: A model pretrained on broad data at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks rather than trained for a single one [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. The term comes from machine learning, and this chapter treats such a model as one optional component inside a design system rather than as the design system itself.

Our initial paper set out the broad Architecture 2.0 vision across system and chip design [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. To ground the engineering arguments across this monograph, we define Architecture 2.0 not as a speculative claim of automated autonomy, but as a disciplined design and evidence standard:

> **Architecture 2.0.** Architecture 2.0 is the discipline of building AI-native design systems that carry high-level system intent across the hardware–software boundary toward supported architecture results, and of holding those systems to an architecture-grade evidence standard. It shifts the architect's primary role from manually crafting point microarchitectures to formulating multi-objective constraints, managing automated exploration, and delivering technical recommendations that a named commitment authority can review.

The historical evolution of design methodology reveals a continuous migration of manual effort into automated tools, paired with an elevation in the human architect's evaluative responsibility. Three distinct epochs characterize how architectural automation and human decision authority have co-evolved (@tbl-architecture-epochs), progressing from physical drafting in the transistor era to structured abstractions and, ultimately, to closed-loop AI-native design systems:

| **Epoch and Era** | **Fundamental Paradigm** | **AI and Automation Mechanism** | **Primary Human Role** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Architecture 0.0**<br/>(Transistor Era) | Physical Construction | Manual schematics, layout design rules, and unassisted computer-aided design (CAD) scripts | Drafting polygons and wiring circuits |
| **Architecture 1.0**<br/>(Mead–Conway / H&P Era) | Structured Abstraction | **Pre-2016:** Logic synthesis and branch perceptrons<br/><br/>**2016–2021 (Deep Learning Era):** Task-specific surrogates and point CAD optimization | Hand-crafting specifications and evaluating point designs |
| **Architecture 2.0**<br/>(Emerging AI-Native Discipline) | Closed-Loop Architecture Work | **Current capability:** Foundation models, learned surrogates, and early multi-tool orchestration<br/><br/>**Program target:** Closed-loop design systems that connect intent to checked architecture results | Formulating intent, setting bounds, forming recommendations, and retaining named commitment authority |
: **Architecture epochs trace the migration from manual drafting to closed-loop search.** Each epoch moves work from the architect's hands into the tools, and moves the architect toward bounding the search and owning the commitment. Automation runs from unassisted CAD scripts through localized learned surrogates toward closed-loop design systems. The final row states an emerging engineering program rather than a completed historical transition. {#tbl-architecture-epochs tbl-colwidths="[20,25,30,25]"}

Across these epochs, the architect's role shifts from drafting individual physical artifacts to formulating multi-objective constraints and exercising commitment authority. Distinguishing where and how automated methods participate in architectural design establishes three operational layers of AI capability (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration):

- **Layer 1: AI-Assisted Engineering (Point-Task Acceleration).** Deploying learned models, foundation tools, or generative heuristics to accelerate isolated human drafting and analysis tasks within an established engineering workflow. Examples include generating boilerplate RTL modules, drafting SystemVerilog assertions, parsing static timing logs, or summarizing design documentation. In Layer 1, the human engineer remains the sole integration engine, manually debugging synthesis warnings, reconciling interface widths, and hunting race conditions in waveform viewers. Because generation velocity does not alter surrounding data representations, verification harnesses, or physical signoff boundaries, human review forms an unscaled bottleneck that caps workflow speedup under Amdahl's law.
- **Layer 2: AI-Driven Subsystem Optimization (Deep Local Search).** Deploying autonomous closed-loop search (such as reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization, or surrogate cost models) within a fixed, pre-bounded architectural container. Notable industrial examples include reinforcement-learning-driven macro floorplanning [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], autotuning graphics processing unit (GPU) kernel tile configurations, optimizing compiler phase ordering, and tuning dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) controller scheduling policies. While Layer 2 executes autonomous closed-loop search, human architects freeze the subsystem boundary. Because the optimizer operates within fixed interfaces, it cannot evaluate cross-layer trade-offs. If an automated floorplan suffers unroutable routing congestion, the optimizer cannot refactor the pipeline or shift an algorithmic step into the compiler; its gains remain trapped inside the frozen container envelope.
- **Layer 3: AI-Native System Design (Cross-Boundary System Orchestration).** Structuring the complete vertical design stack around multi-tool closed-loop search, machine-usable intermediate representations (IRs, such as Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect lowering [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR; @SiliconCompiler]), and rejectable multi-fidelity verification harnesses. Rather than optimizing within a frozen container or assisting an isolated drafting step, an AI-native design system searches across workload requirements, compiler representations, microarchitectural parameters, and physical signoff checks. The search loop remains strictly bounded by the physical and formal tools that actually ran, operating under in-order human commitment authority.

![**The three operational layers of AI in system and chip design.** The architectural hierarchy distinguishes point-task acceleration (Layer 1) and deep local subsystem optimization (Layer 2) from cross-boundary system orchestration (Layer 3). Layer 1 accelerates isolated human drafting tasks within existing manual workflows. Layer 2 executes autonomous closed-loop search inside a fixed, pre-bounded subsystem container. Layer 3 structures the entire exploration workflow across the hardware–software stack around multi-tool orchestration, machine-usable state representations, and rejectable verification harnesses under in-order human commitment authority. The Architecture 2.0 moonshot operates at Layer 3.](images/fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration){#fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration width="100%" fig-alt="Three-layer architectural hierarchy diagram comparing Layer 1 AI-assisted engineering, Layer 2 AI-driven subsystem optimization, and Layer 3 AI-native system design across operational scope, technical mechanisms, and governance signoff boundaries."}

Studying this progression requires explicit operational definitions of *architecture*, *architect*, and *commitment authority*. Architecture encompasses far more than a novel microarchitecture, a high-level block diagram, or an isolated physical chip artifact:

> **Architecture.** Architecture is the hardware and software contract and system organization turning workload intent and technology constraints into a defensible system design. It includes the instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory, interconnects, accelerators, chiplets, compiler and runtime interfaces, and deployment model.

> **Architect.** The architect is responsible for the architecture recommendation within the project's decision structure. The architect frames the problem, chooses abstractions, sets the evidence standard, integrates cross-layer results, and forms the supported technical recommendation. Specialists qualify measurements and checks and own technical signoffs in their domains.

The architect recommends; someone must still decide, and that decision requires its own operational boundary. *In-Order Commit Authority* (or *Commitment Authority*) denotes the strict organizational decision threshold wherein a designated human authority holds exclusive, nondelegable approval rights to advance an architectural recommendation across a consequential transition, ensuring that automated generators never commit silicon capital or modify baseline contracts out of order. Conceptually, this threshold functions like an in-order instruction commit unit in an out-of-order microprocessor pipeline. While execution units (generative models and search algorithms) speculate aggressively and propose candidate results in parallel, only the named commitment authority can retire decisions into permanent architectural state. The architect supplies the supported technical recommendation. One person may hold both roles, but the organization must assign each responsibility and approval right explicitly. Automated methods can contribute candidates and analysis without assuming either responsibility.

Computer architecture has long embraced learned mechanisms inside hardware blocks, ranging from perceptron branch predictors, later adopted in shipping silicon, to surrogate models used in design-space exploration [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron; @IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE]. However, the focus throughout this monograph is not on embedding neural components into silicon datapaths, but rather on building Layer 3 AI-native design systems that elevate the engineering practice of architecture design itself, coordinating cross-layer search under rigorous verification contracts.

## The 2030 Moonshot Goal

The term *moonshot* draws an explicit parallel to historical engineering milestones such as the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Grand Challenge for autonomous vehicles.[^fn-darpa-grand-challenge-c01] In 2004, the initial DARPA competition saw every robotic vehicle fail or flip within miles of the start line. By 2005, autonomous systems navigated 132\ miles of rugged desert terrain because engineering teams stopped tuning isolated sensor heuristics and built tightly integrated, closed-loop perception and actuation systems [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley]. In computer architecture, an architecture moonshot defines a similarly rigorous milestone. It requires building a closed-loop design system that carries compact system intent through multi-objective exploration, real toolchains, and physical signoff to produce defensible hardware-and-software results.

An engineering challenge with these properties must be broad enough to stress multiple subsystems while remaining grounded in real workloads and physical signoff. To anchor the methodology across this monograph, we establish a concrete, representative moonshot challenge:

> **The Lighthouse Moonshot Goal.** By 2030, an AI-native design system will automatically take a high-level system prompt, decompose it across compiler, microarchitecture, and circuit layers, and produce an optimized, verified system-on-chip that achieves human-expert-grade power, performance, and area (PPA) while meeting all physical signoff contracts.

We ground this goal in a concrete, end-to-end design study carried throughout this book: designing a real-time compute subsystem for a next-generation mobile extended-reality (XR) headset under a strict 3\ W power envelope. Rather than treating this prompt as an abstract ambition, @sec-intent-vs-spec decomposes it into explicit, machine-usable requirements across the eight domains of modern architecture design. An architecture moonshot becomes testable when real workload demands force a change in design methodology. Rather than optimizing unconstrained synthetic benchmarks, a rigorous study must evaluate whether learned methods can close timing on advanced process nodes, satisfy strict thermal envelopes, and vectorize domain kernels while recording the physical measurements that would falsify candidate claims.

[^fn-darpa-grand-challenge-c01]: **DARPA Grand Challenge (origin)**: The 2004–2007 Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency prize competitions transformed autonomous vehicle engineering from isolated laboratory algorithms into integrated systems capable of navigating complex physical environments under real-world operational constraints; the 2005 Grand Challenge and its winning vehicle are the documented anchor [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley].

::: {.callout-design-principle title="An architecture moonshot must expand expressible and checkable design space"}
**The principle:** An architecture moonshot defines a systemic, verifiable advance in translating compact intent into physically realizable hardware-and-software results.

**The rationale:** Adding automation to an unconstrained or unverified design loop generates candidate artifacts faster without expanding what an architecture team can systematically prove or defend. An architecture moonshot succeeds only when it expands the scale of expressible design intent and binds that intent to repeatable, independent physical and software verification infrastructure.
:::

## The Architecture Moonshot Brief

Testing cross-stack decision-making requires an industrial challenge that couples aggressive physical constraints with heterogeneous compute engines. This investigation centers on a mobile XR system-on-chip (SoC) subsystem, evaluating whether learned tools can negotiate trade-offs that span compiler software, microarchitecture, and physical silicon implementation. In industrial practice, architecture studies rarely start with formal, machine-executable specifications. Instead, they begin with a compact product request that compresses complex physical and computational expectations into a few sentences. Decomposing this high-level prompt exposes dependencies that span every layer of the hardware–software stack.

### The Mobile XR Subsystem Case Study

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse prompt"}
Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class
real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable CPU, accelerator,
or SoC block under a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) target in a 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process, and
return a design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives.
:::

The Lighthouse prompt serves as a standardized, multi-constraint benchmark request that articulates compact system intent to guide AI-native design-space exploration across realistic hardware, software, and physical boundaries. The case study adopts XRBench [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] because it offers a public suite of mobile XR workloads rather than a rigid, proprietary product specification. Operating at this scale exposes the architectural friction that smaller code-generation tasks obscure. A complete architecture study decomposes the compact Lighthouse prompt into three structural dimensions: the high-level product prompt, the eight coupled requirement domains it implies, and the execution and analysis pipeline required to support a technical recommendation (@fig-moonshot-prompt).

![**Compact system prompts encapsulate multi-layer architecture studies.** The compact Lighthouse prompt (top) decomposes into eight coupled architectural requirement domains (middle: workload, ISA/ABI, compute organization, memory hierarchy, power envelope, compiler/runtime, physical node, and reliability/verification), which drive the multi-fidelity simulation, synthesis, and physical signoff pipeline (bottom) required to substantiate a technical recommendation for commitment authority review.](images/fig-moonshot-prompt){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="100%" fig-alt="Stacked diagram with the full Lighthouse prompt at the top, architecture requirements in the middle, and the execution and analysis requirements needed to support an answer at the bottom."}

Lowering high-level intent into an executable design study requires addressing dependencies across eight tightly coupled architectural requirement domains, where downstream tool feedback exposes violations and enforces physical bounds:

1. **Workload domain:** Real-time mobile XR workloads drawn from XRBench [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench], complemented by SPEC CPU2017 [@SPEC2017CPU] traces and MLPerf [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf] inference kernels.
2. **ISA and ABI contract domain:** A 64-bit RISC-V application processor core (RV64GCV) equipped with a 128-bit RISC-V Vector (RVV) 1.0 execution pipeline, bound by a standardized application binary interface (ABI).
3. **Compute organization domain:** A heterogeneous combination of a vector-capable CPU core, a dedicated neural processing unit (NPU) systolic matrix engine, and specialized SoC blocks.
4. **Memory and data movement domain:** A multi-level cache hierarchy (32\ KiB L1 caches, an explored 2\ MiB L2 cache, and a 4\ MiB shared system-level L3 cache) paired with tightly coupled memory (TCM) scratchpads. On-chip traffic routes over an Arm Microcontroller Bus Architecture (AMBA) Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) on-chip interconnect with verified network-on-chip (NoC) bisection bandwidth, while modular chiplet attachments and off-chip memory connect through Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) interfaces and dedicated LPDDR5X DRAM controllers under strict timing constraints.
5. **Power envelope domain:** A 3\ W sustained TDP target operating under passive optical frame cooling and skin-temperature ceilings (below $41^\circ\text{C}$).[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]
6. **Compiler and runtime stack domain:** Software execution paths transformed from abstract syntax trees (ASTs) and control data flow graphs (CDFGs) through intermediate representation (IR) compiler frameworks and domain libraries with vector intrinsics, meeting rigid 8.33\ ms frame deadlines at 120\ frames per second (FPS) [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR].
7. **Physical constraints domain:** Implementation targets framed in 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process nodes.
8. **Reliability and verification domain:** Signoff guarantees combining formal property verification for protocol compliance, low-power domain isolation intent under Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF), and static timing closure across process corners.

[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]: **Mobile XR and Smart Glasses Thermal Boundaries**: Wearable spatial computing systems, ranging from ultralightweight smart glasses to high-performance spatial headsets such as the current Meta and Apple devices, face hard physical constraints in human skin-temperature safety limits (roughly $41^\circ\text{C}$) and passive frame heat dissipation. In smart glasses and wearable spatial platforms, the total system power envelope must stay under roughly 2\ W to 3\ W TDP to prevent thermal throttling and skin discomfort against human temples. Achieving continuous spatial perception, eye-tracking, and neural rendering within such an envelope requires combining low-power mobile silicon nodes (such as TSMC N3E or N7) with energy-efficient on-chip AXI5 NoC interconnects, 2.5D/3D UCIe die stacking, and LPDDR5X memory interfaces.

Mobile XR is an ideal target because it couples tight latency, thermal, and energy constraints with complex cross-layer behavior. In a wearable headset resting millimeters from human skin, thermal dissipation is strictly passive; exceeding the $41^\circ\text{C}$ surface limit causes thermal throttling, frame drops, or physical discomfort. Optimizing a single kernel or hardware block without accounting for the software pipeline, memory hierarchy, or frame deadlines degrades user experience [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. Early bring-up of this software stack and ISA contract relies on functional simulators such as Spike and Renode to verify compiler behavior before hardware implementation begins. Integrating intellectual property (IP) blocks into an SoC introduces strict interface requirements. An accelerator must interface with host infrastructure through standard protocols such as AMBA AXI [@Arm2020AXI]. If an automated generator optimizes local cycle count by omitting backpressure logic on the `ARREADY` or `AWREADY` handshake channels (such as assuming zero wait states or driving `VALID` without registering `READY`), the candidate may look exceptionally fast in an isolated synthetic testbench, but will deadlock the entire on-chip interconnect the moment multiple engines contend for DRAM. A candidate that exhibits superior nominal PPA metrics while violating an AXI handshake contract is not a viable optimization; it is broken silicon.

A prompt expresses compact intent, but engineering execution requires formal precision. Requirements translate high-level intent into concrete bounds, including target clock frequencies, memory bandwidth limits, and vector register widths. The specification pins down ISA opcodes, AXI bus interfaces, and benchmark traces (such as XRBench simultaneous localization and mapping [SLAM] kernels), while the study plan fixes the baseline CPU, simulator configurations (such as Spike and gem5), and budget limits before running exploration. Terms such as "XRBench-class," "3\ W," and "3\ nm-class" in the Lighthouse prompt require concrete versioned workloads, process assumptions, and verification checks. Architects must explicitly resolve these unstated parameters before this request can drive real engineering, deciding which interpretation enters the specification and what constitutes a successful result.

On this Lighthouse study, the three operational layers produce starkly different engineering actions (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration). At Layer 1, an engineer prompts a foundation model to draft an isolated RTL module (such as a systolic matrix multiply-accumulate [MAC] unit or AXI bus interface), manually debugging the generated Verilog in their local editor. At Layer 2, an autonomous optimizer tunes a fixed subsystem container (such as searching processing element [PE] array dimensions in SCALE-Sim or optimizing an L2 cache bank schedule), but remains blind to compiler lowering passes, DRAM bank contention, or full-subsystem power envelopes. At Layer 3, the complete design system coordinates multi-tool exploration across all eight requirement domains (spanning XRBench workload kernels down through MLIR lowering, RTL synthesis, static timing, and formal assertion checking), delivering a verifiable recommendation under human commitment authority.

Answering this prompt requires a memory trace gathered from a fixed XRBench configuration, a compiler targeting the proposed organization, a calibrated simulator, a synthesis run mapped to a low-power library, and expert reviewers who verify that the results substantiate the recommendation. Throughout this book, the object of study is the complete human-plus-technical workflow rather than the fluency of an isolated generated response. Where closed-loop studies lack complete physical signoff or matched baseline evidence, the study records report the status as unresolved; holding an AI-native design system to an architecture-grade evidence standard requires the discipline to report where evidence stops.

### Decomposing Intent into Executable Specifications {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

A compact product prompt conceals deep cross-stack dependencies that an engineering team must explicitly resolve before executing downstream tools. Turning high-level requirements into an executable specification demands formal contracts across every level of the design hierarchy, from instruction encodings to physical signoff decks (@fig-moonshot-prompt). Without these concrete bounds, automated search tools either exploit ambiguous defaults or optimize for metrics that fail physical implementation.

First, the ISA and microarchitecture scope must be bound. Specifying a "64-bit RISC-V compute subsystem" fixes the RV64GCV base ISA, but requires explicit decisions on vector register lengths, matrix extensions, ABI conventions,[^fn-abi-c01] and runtime software contracts. The prompt allows multiple compute organizations, spanning scalar cores, decoupled vector pipelines, and specialized systolic NPU engines.

Second, the *Hardware Semantic Gap* separates natural language intent from cycle-exact, bit-deterministic silicon. Software engineering can absorb runtime ambiguities through dynamic memory allocation, duck typing, and exception handlers. In hardware design, natural language underspecifies exact signal transitions across three strict physical-contract layers:

- **Signal and Timing Integrity:** When asynchronous clock domains meet without dual-rank synchronizers, metastable flip-flop resolution times exceed clock periods, latching nondeterministic intermediate logic levels into downstream state machines. Similarly, unsynchronized reset domain crossings (RDCs) violate recovery and removal timing, leaving flip-flops in arbitrary, uncoordinated power-on states that prevent deterministic boot sequences.
- **Interface and Memory Protocols:** A generated controller that misinterprets valid-ready handshake rules on an AMBA AXI bus (such as making `VALID` combinatorially dependent on `READY` or dropping unacknowledged flits) creates transient deadlock conditions. In addition, code generators that assume sequential consistency fail when the host processor enforces the weaker RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO) model, allowing memory operations to execute out of intended order.
- **Physical Power Domains:** Multi-voltage designs governed by IEEE 1801 UPF rules require explicit level shifters and isolation cells. An unisolated interface crossing from a powered-down rail into an active domain leaves inputs floating in the high-gain intermediate voltage region ($V_{tn} < V_{in} < V_{dd} - |V_{tp}|$). This turns on both PMOS and NMOS networks simultaneously, drawing massive short-circuit crowbar current and triggering destructive complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) latchup in fabricated silicon.

Third, physical and thermal limits bound the search space in advanced semiconductor nodes. Achieving a 3\ W TDP in a mobile XR form factor requires explicit models for passive frame heat dissipation, skin-temperature ceilings (below $41^\circ\text{C}$), static random-access memory (SRAM)-to-DRAM area trade-offs, NoC bisection bandwidth, and off-chip memory access energy. In leading-edge sub-3\ nm-class nodes, classical scaling has stalled. While intrinsic gate switching speed continues to see modest improvements ($\approx 10\text{--}15\%$), exponential resistance growth in sub-24\ nm pitch lower-metal interconnects ($M_0\text{--}M_2$) (driven by electron surface scattering and grain-boundary scattering as wire cross-sections shrink below the copper electron mean free path) causes parasitic $RC$ wire delay to dominate cycle times. Concurrently, standard 6T SRAM bitcell scaling has hit a physical plateau, shrinking by less than 5% from 5\ nm to 3\ nm (remaining near $0.021\ \mu\text{m}^2$) due to transistor aspect-ratio limits and minimum static noise margins (SNM). Sizing on-chip SRAM buffers thus becomes a direct physical area, routing congestion, and thermal trade-off. Because mobile XR subsystems continuously ingest sensitive biometric and spatial sensor streams, the Reliability and verification domain requires declared threat models, physical-memory access controls, and side-channel defenses. While RISC-V Physical Memory Protection (PMP) enforces physical-memory access permissions, it does not close timing or shared-cache side channels [@RISCV2026PrivilegedISA].

[^fn-abi-c01]: **ABI (application binary interface)**: The binary-level agreement on register usage, calling conventions, stack layout, and data alignment that lets separately compiled code interoperate. Adding a custom instruction changes the ISA, but shipping it means the compiler, libraries, and operating system have to agree on the ABI as well, which is why an ISA extension is a software project rather than a hardware edit.

Fourth, multi-objective design choices require evaluating the Pareto frontier [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. A final study report connects candidate artifacts, Pareto-optimal sets, and physical measurements, documenting why rejected alternatives failed baseline criteria. A product request does not supply a 3\ W budget or specify an L2 cache capacity; architects derive those constraints by coupling analytical models, profiling data, and physical limits.

Point AI assistance can accelerate this formulation by extracting candidate constraints from requirement documents, checking consistency against past designs, and surfacing ambiguities (such as clarifying whether "real-time" means an 8.33\ ms frame deadline at 120\ Hz or a 99th-percentile tail-latency bound). However, point assistance does not replace architectural judgment. Architects must validate the proposed bounds and express accepted constraints in machine-readable formats that downstream tools can ingest.

Foundry process declarations demand equal precision. While the prompt specifies a "3\ nm-class" process, physical signoff requires a specific foundry process design kit (PDK),[^fn-pdk-c01] cell libraries, operating voltages, and signoff corners [@Apple2024A18Pro; @Apple2024M4]. Commercial PDKs operate under strict foundry nondisclosure agreements, meaning automated generative pipelines must operate within secure, air-gapped data governance boundaries. Early screening may use calibrated analytical models, but physical feasibility claims require full EDA toolchain execution.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **PDK (process design kit)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. The open SKY130 PDK demonstrates that a PDK can be published [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], but it cannot supply the authorized project-specific information for a different process or commercial tool flow.

Across all these layers, the software stack acts as the limiting dependency. Adding a specialized 128-bit vector unit or systolic matrix accelerator to the mobile XR subsystem is useless if the compiler framework (such as MLIR dialects or LLVM backends) cannot automatically tile, vectorize, and schedule the XRBench pose-estimation kernels onto that datapath. Meeting workload and physical constraints requires an AI-native design system that keeps compiler representations, hardware generators, and review loops tightly coupled across all eight requirement domains.

## AI Models vs. AI-Native Design Systems

Navigating these cross-layer dependencies requires separating the tools engineering teams train from the design systems they operate. A foundation model or learned surrogate is a stateless tool component that proposes candidates or accelerates estimation; it holds no live project memory, cannot verify physical constraints, and cannot issue architectural commitments. In contrast, an AI-native design system represents the complete technical capability, coupling learned components with version-controlled project state, deterministic simulators, EDA toolchains, and formal verification engines under human commitment authority (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). Three core concepts anchor this distinction across technical workflows:

1. **Architecture foundation models:** Pretrained learned components [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels] that supply reusable prior knowledge across multiple tasks (such as workload classification or heuristic search guidance) without live project state or commitment authority.
2. **AI-native design systems:** The configured technical ensemble of learned models, conventional simulators, versioned artifacts, tool interfaces, feedback loops, and automated verification checks.
3. **Version-controlled project state:** The immutable source of record, maintaining machine-readable specifications, SystemVerilog RTL, C++ behavioral models, and physical layout scripts.

An AI-native design system couples a reusable knowledge substrate with deterministic project state and independent human authority (@fig-foundation-system). In the Lighthouse study, learned models propose candidate organizations, generate draft RTL, or triage simulation diagnostics. However, the authoritative project record supplies the exact workload trace, power envelope, candidate identifiers, and pinned tool versions. These immutable inputs govern what simulators, implementation tools, and signoff flows actually evaluate; no pretrained model can substitute for them.

![**Foundation models function as optional components within the broader design system.** Reusable architecture knowledge can support a learned component adapted to workload analysis, prediction, generation, or diagnosis, while the immutable project record, conventional methods, simulators, EDA tools, and formal checks govern active tasks [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Architects supply intent and constraints, review the supported result, and form a technical recommendation, while a separate commitment authority decides whether to advance, hold, or reject the recommendation.](images/fig-foundation-system){#fig-foundation-system width="100%" fig-alt="Reusable architecture knowledge feeds an optional architecture foundation model inside an AI-native design system. A separate version-controlled project record informs the active architecture tasks and conventional methods. Task outputs reach design tools and checks, which return evidence and update project state. A supported architecture result leaves the technical system for review by the architecture role, which forms a supported technical recommendation for a separate commitment authority."}

## What Qualifies as an Architecture Result

Once an AI-native design system couples project state with downstream tools, transforming candidate proposals into verifiable architectural evidence requires a structured evaluation framework. Because generative models can produce candidate code far faster than conventional tools can simulate or physically implement them, architects must balance proxy estimation against high-fidelity verification through rejectable decision loops.

### Qualifying Artifacts into Verifiable Results

Architectural progress moves through a deliberate hierarchy of evidence. High-level intent must expand into concrete specifications, candidate artifacts, empirical observations, and verified comparative results before supporting any commitment decision. This progression distinguishes raw generated outputs from substantiated engineering findings:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Compact Intent} &\longrightarrow \text{Executable Spec} \longrightarrow \text{Candidate Artifact} \\
&\longrightarrow \text{Physical Measurement} \longrightarrow \text{Architecture Result} \longrightarrow \text{Human Commitment}
\end{aligned}$$

These concepts remain distinct throughout the design life cycle:

- **Artifact:** Any concrete output produced during the study (code, RTL, a model, a layout, a report, or a testbench).
- **Candidate:** A proposed design or configuration evaluated within the study.
- **Measurement (or observation):** Empirical data gathered from evaluating a candidate under declared conditions.
- **Architecture result:** A supported comparison or finding where assumptions, conditions, checks, alternatives, and limits are clear enough to inform the next design action.

A valid architecture result does not require a positive breakthrough. It can reject every candidate, retain the reference design, narrow the scope of inquiry, or conclude that available measurements cannot decide the question. In hardware design, the chasm between a draft artifact and a verified result is particularly treacherous. A generator might propose a custom vector instruction that clears behavioral simulation, only to violate formal equivalence, design rules, timing closure, or thermal limits during physical implementation. Fast surrogate models [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate] screen thousands of floorplans or tile schedules in seconds, but surviving designs must still clear authoritative physical EDA signoff before an organization commits capital to silicon fabrication.

Analytical bounds provide cheap, early rejection filters before invoking expensive simulation. Amdahl's law caps whole-system speedup based on the accelerated workload fraction [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The Roofline model relates candidate operational intensity to peak compute and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline]. Candidates that violate these early bounds need not enter the simulation queue, though surviving designs must still be verified through simulation and physical signoff.

When iterative search optimizes against a fast proxy, it risks gaming the proxy's blind spots [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer; @Cadence2026Joules; @Synopsys2026PrimePower]. If an early estimator fails to account for lower-metal wire congestion or macro placement pin density, an optimizer will eagerly pack SRAM banks into unroutable configurations, reporting illusory 30% performance gains that vanish under actual place-and-route into massive setup-slack violations.[^fn-overfitting-c01] Physical EDA tools expose complex timing paths and routing congestion rather than scalar scores.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting and Proxy Exploitation**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. Proxy exploitation is analogous but distinct; it occurs when search algorithms exploit omissions or modeling errors in an evaluator, embodying Goodhart's law in automated design [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement].

A valid architecture result must explicitly identify the candidate, workload, measurement, check, and bounding conditions under which it holds. Never treat a syntactically valid script or a successful local tool return as evidence that an architecture should change.

### Multi-Metric Trade-Offs and Rejectable Evaluation Loops {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

Supporting an architectural claim for the mobile XR subsystem requires balancing competing physical and computational constraints rather than optimizing a single scalar metric. A valid efficiency claim must capture complete system costs within a defined total-cost boundary, incorporating direct and indirect expenditures (including compute throughput, memory bandwidth, thermal dissipation, EDA tool licenses, verification cycles, and human review overhead) required to achieve useful system work [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer; @HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Local improvements in compute throughput remain meaningless if they shift costs to memory bandwidth, violate thermal envelopes, or impose verification burdens that exceed the project budget.

Data movement exposes this boundary in physical terms. In modern CMOS nodes, arithmetic compute is essentially free, but moving data across wires dominates the thermal budget. In 45\ nm data, a 32-bit integer add costs approximately 0.1\ pJ, while reading those operands from off-chip DRAM costs roughly 1,300\ pJ to 2,000\ pJ: four orders of magnitude more energy [@Horowitz2014Energy]. In a 3\ nm-class mobile XR SoC, off-chip LPDDR5X DRAM accesses across the AMBA AXI5 interconnect heavily pressure the 3\ W TDP envelope. Evaluating an accelerator that increases memory traffic requires a full system energy comparison rather than an isolated compute efficiency metric. Multi-metric evaluation spans five physical system dimensions alongside the meta-cost of the engineering study (@tbl-efficiency-dimensions):

| **Dimension** | **Question** | **Why it complicates the comparison** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Performance** | How much useful work is delivered per unit time, latency budget, or service-level target? | The answer depends on workload selection, scenario, software stack, and whether the measured behavior matches the deployment claim. |
| **Power and energy** | How much useful work is delivered per watt, joule, thermal budget, or battery envelope? | A credible comparison must account for activity, data movement, voltage/frequency choices, thermal constraints, and fidelity gaps between estimates and signoff. |
| **Reliability and correctness** | Which required behaviors hold across faults, corner cases, nondeterminism, and the declared operating conditions? | A faster candidate is not acceptable if it spends its savings on fragility, security side-channels, debug burden, or invalid software and hardware assumptions. |
| **Scalability and cost** | How much useful work is delivered per dollar, rack, network hop, operator action, or unit of capacity? | Local wins can shift cost to memory, network, power delivery, utilization, operations, or total cost of ownership. |
| **Sustainability** | How much useful work is delivered per unit of operational and embodied environmental footprint? | Carbon depends on hardware lifetime, manufacturing, energy mix, utilization, and where and when computation runs. |
| **Study cost: evidence and engineering effort** | How much decision-relevant evidence is obtained per simulation, experiment, verification run, or engineer-hour? | Generating more candidates can still be inefficient if evaluation consumes scarce feedback, hides failures, or cannot reject weak outputs. |
: **A system result and the work needed to establish it require different measures.** Five dimensions describe the proposed system, while evidence and engineering effort describe the study. A valid comparison must show when an apparent improvement shifts cost or changes the scope. {#tbl-efficiency-dimensions tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

In the mobile XR setting anchored by XRBench and ILLIXR [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR], frame latency, energy, sustained power, and data movement are tightly coupled. Measured RTL generation benchmarks exhibit severe functional pass-rate attrition [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval], proving that generated code cannot bypass independent verification harnesses. The practical test is whether the complete design system, including its verification overhead, improves the architectural result or lowers total engineering cost relative to competent conventional baselines.

## State of the Art and Benchmark Assessment

Current design automation tools reveal a sharp divergence between rapid candidate proposal generation and slow physical verification. While learned methods accelerate localized exploration and drafting, end-to-end progress remains bounded by downstream simulation and signoff capacity. Mapping these capabilities across the design hierarchy clarifies where automated techniques succeed today and where fundamental verification bottlenecks persist.

### Survey of AI-Assisted Design Tools

Existing AI-assisted design tools demonstrate strong point capabilities within specific evaluation regimes rather than a unified, end-to-end autonomous flow. Recent efforts span exact mathematical search, hardware autotuning, learned physical macro placement, proxy-guided design space exploration, and automated RTL generation. As mapped in the taxonomy in @sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map, each system establishes progress within a specific evaluation domain, yet every result remains bounded by the fidelity and scope of its underlying verification checks.

These efforts represent point AI assistance; they accelerate isolated steps in search, placement, or code generation while leaving surrounding workflows unchanged. In software engineering, evaluation frameworks such as SWE-bench [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] execute test suites in seconds, yielding immediate pass-fail feedback for candidate patches. Hardware design evaluation operates in an entirely different physical regime. A candidate cannot be validated by a clean unit-test run alone; full hardware signoff demands multi-corner physical synthesis, formal equivalence checking, static timing analysis, and thermal modeling. Fast proxies prune unpromising candidates, but only physical and formal checks can qualify a design before an organization commits capital to masks.

Computer architecture possesses shared benchmarks and simulation infrastructure at individual layers: SPEC CPU2017 [@SPEC2017CPU] standardizes CPU performance evaluations, gem5 [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5] and FireSim [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim] provide cycle-accurate and field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-accelerated simulation, and MLPerf [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf] standardizes machine-learning evaluation. These resources ensure outside researchers can rerun and challenge scoped results, but they do not connect all the cross-stack evidence required for the Lighthouse. Current systems establish bounded point progress rather than an end-to-end automated flow.

### The Verification Asymmetry {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

AI-assisted hardware design starts from an impoverished data foundation compared to software engineering. Open-source software corpora contain hundreds of billions of tokens across mature production codebases, while public hardware repositories contain barely 3.8\ GB of uncurated HDL files across all hardware description languages combined [@LozhkovEtAl2024TheStackV2; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet; @PrakashEtAl2025QuArch; @ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. These units are not directly comparable, but they demonstrate why an AI-native design system requires task-specific curation and machine-checkable evidence rather than assuming broad software pretraining covers architecture work (@sec-data-representations-world-models).

Hardware design is also heavily guarded by proprietary process design kits and confidential IP blocks [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. Relying solely on models trained on public corpora produces plausible-looking RTL that misses project-specific interfaces, foundry PDKs, and signoff constraints. Training data provenance directly affects legal compliance. Generating RTL from unverified public code risks IP contamination and subtle hardware trojans, while sending proprietary netlists to external model APIs risks trade-secret disclosure. Managing source permissions, output provenance, confidentiality, and external review access is a nonnegotiable data governance requirement.

Better project information improves what a generator proposes without settling whether the proposal is physically correct. A first-pass RTL candidate can look syntactically flawless while concealing subtle, fatal timing races or functional deadlocks; the true distance between a generated artifact and a supported result is measured in executed verification checks rather than generated lines of code. Published generation benchmarks report severe attrition at parsing, interface compliance, and functional simulation stages [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet], compounding through timing closure and layout checks into a narrow survival funnel (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). As design scope expands, candidate proposal latency and verification check time diverge by orders of magnitude (@fig-verification-scaling). While proposal generation stays under one minute across abstraction levels, downstream verification scales from milliseconds for tensor operators to days or weeks for full SoC signoff and formal equivalence checking.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-scaling
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Proposing a candidate and checking one do not scale together.** Across five design abstraction
#|   levels (tensor operators, core microarchitecture, RTL block signoff, subsystem macros, and full SoC
#|   signoff), candidate proposal latency remains under one minute while verification check time scales
#|   from milliseconds (AutoTVM/MAESTRO) to days or weeks (Cadence/Formality full SoC signoff), opening a
#|   four-order-of-magnitude verification gap. Constructed order-of-magnitude ranges, not per-candidate
#|   measurements; a project's specific EDA tool flow sets where the separation lands.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart comparing AI candidate proposal latency against hardware verification check time across five design scales from tensor operators to full SoC signoff. Verification check time scales from milliseconds to days/weeks, while AI candidate generation remains under one minute."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
import numpy as np

apply_style()

categories = [
    "Tensor Operator\n(AutoTVM / MAESTRO)",
    "Core Microarch\n(gem5 / Spike)",
    "RTL Block Signoff\n(Verilator / Yosys)",
    "Subsystem Macro\n(OpenROAD 7nm)",
    "Full SoC Signoff\n(Cadence / Formality)",
]
y_pos = np.arange(len(categories))
eval_latency_min = np.array([0.001, 10.0, 300.0, 3600.0, 86400.0])
eval_latency_max = np.array([0.1, 300.0, 3600.0, 28800.0, 604800.0])
gen_latency = np.array([0.5, 2.0, 5.0, 15.0, 45.0])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.28, right=0.94, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

for i in range(len(categories)):
    ax.barh(
        y_pos[i] + 0.15,
        eval_latency_max[i] - eval_latency_min[i],
        left=eval_latency_min[i],
        height=0.35,
        color=COLORS["constraints"],
        alpha=0.85,
        edgecolor=COLORS["constraints_ink"],
        linewidth=0.8,
        label="Hardware verification check time" if i == 0 else "",
        zorder=2,
    )

ax.scatter(
    gen_latency,
    y_pos - 0.15,
    color=COLORS["workload"],
    s=48,
    zorder=4,
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
    label="AI candidate proposal latency",
)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
ax.set_yticklabels(categories, fontsize=6.2, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.invert_yaxis()

ax.set_xlabel("Time per candidate (seconds, log scale)", fontsize=6.5, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.set_xlim(1e-4, 1e6)

xticks = [1e-3, 1e-1, 10, 3600, 86400, 604800]
xtick_labels = ["1 ms", "100 ms", "10 s", "1 hour", "1 day", "1 week"]
ax.set_xticks(xticks)
ax.set_xticklabels(xtick_labels, fontsize=5.8)


leg = ax.legend(frameon=True, facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"], edgecolor=COLORS["note_edge"], fontsize=5.8, loc="upper right", framealpha=1.0)
leg.set_zorder(10)
ax.grid(True, which="both", axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)

ax.annotate(
    "4-order-of-magnitude\nverification gap",
    xy=(1e4, 3.85),
    xytext=(5e-3, 1.8),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], lw=0.9),
    fontsize=6.0,
    fontweight="bold",
    color=COLORS["constraints_ink"],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"], edgecolor=COLORS["constraints"], lw=0.8),
    zorder=12,

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

Hardware security verification extends far beyond functional instruction conformance. As Spectre demonstrated, microarchitectures that are 100% architecturally compliant with the ISA manual can still leak cryptographic keys across security domains through speculative execution and transient timing side channels [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. If an automated generator synthesizes an out-of-order execution engine without explicit microarchitectural security verification, it will eagerly exploit speculation windows or shared cache lines to optimize throughput metrics, re-introducing side-channel vulnerabilities that compromise isolation. Generating hardware with learned models requires independent, adversarial checks tailored to the system threat model: verifying physical domain isolation, analyzing cache timing channels, and detecting structural or malicious anomalies. Because physical and security signoff checks cannot be bypassed, scaling automated exploration requires fundamentally restructuring how engineering teams define tasks, state representations, and decision boundaries.

## From Architecture 1.0 to Architecture 2.0 {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

Bridging this four-order-of-magnitude verification gap without surrendering human decision authority requires fundamentally restructuring the operational discipline of computer architecture [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Architecture 1.0 relies on the engineer to hold state in their head and manually bridge disparate tool runs through analytical models, scripted parameter sweeps, and manual microarchitectural tuning. Architecture 2.0 explicitly structures machine-usable project state and bounded action spaces, incorporating learned generation, surrogate prediction, and agentic search across the hardware–software boundary. This transition shifts the architect's primary role from crafting individual point designs to formulating system constraints, managing automated exploration, and delivering supported technical recommendations for the named commitment authority. Five core responsibilities contrast established Architecture 1.0 practice with AI-native Architecture 2.0 methodology (@tbl-arch1-vs-arch2):

| **Feature** | **Established architecture practice (Architecture 1.0)** | **AI-native architecture practice (Architecture 2.0)** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Problem framing | Architects define the question, abstractions, constraints, and tool tasks | Learned methods may help interpret broader intent or incomplete information and propose choices for architect review |
| Exploration | Architects use analytical models, scripts, parameterized generators, sweeps, and conventional optimization | Prediction, generation, and learned optimization may propose, screen, or select alternatives alongside established methods |
| Tool use | Architects and scripts invoke simulators and design tools, preserve results, and decide what to run next | Automated components may select later actions from tool returns, so state, cost, failures, and permitted actions must be usable by the component and inspectable by the reviewer |
| Result standard | Measurements and checks turn candidate artifacts into comparisons that can support the next architecture action | The same standard applies; broader automated participation does not make an unchecked artifact an architecture result |
| Recommendation and commitment | Architects integrate results and form the technical recommendation; a named commitment authority decides whether the architecture advances to the next consequential transition | Methods may organize analysis or prepare a draft recommendation, while the architect and commitment authority retain their respective responsibilities |
: **AI participation broadens what may be delegated without changing the authority structure.** Architecture 2.0 adds learned prediction, generation, optimization, retrieval, or tool coordination to established analytical and automated practice, while the architect and commitment authority retain their respective decision-making roles. {#tbl-arch1-vs-arch2 tbl-colwidths="[18,41,41]"}

Integrating automated agents into the design loop requires structuring machine-usable project state and action spaces while preserving explicit human review boundaries (@fig-design-loop-breaks). In established human-orchestrated studies, project knowledge remains distributed across specifications, source code, tool databases, and expert practice, whereas AI-native systems explicitly formalize selected state and permitted action spaces for machine execution without delegating organizational commitment authority.

![**Automated participation introduces explicit machine-use representation requirements.** In established human-orchestrated studies (left), project knowledge remains distributed across specifications, source code, tool databases, verification artifacts, and expert practice. In AI-native design systems (right), selected state and permitted action spaces are explicitly structured for machine consumption while remaining fully inspectable by human reviewers. Both panels retain an architect review point and closed-loop feedback path without delegating organizational commitment authority to automated components [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20].](images/fig-design-loop-breaks){#fig-design-loop-breaks width="100%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side diagrams compare established human-orchestrated studies and studies run inside an AI-native design system. The left distributes project knowledge across engineering artifacts, records, and expert practice. The right also represents selected state and permitted actions for automated methods. Both panels retain explicit evidence, expert or architect review, and a feedback path without assigning organizational commitment to the review step."}

The central structural shift in @fig-design-loop-breaks is the formal representation of project state and permitted action spaces for machine consumption. Instead of requiring engineers to manually adjust EDA flags and rerun scripts in terminals, the AI-native design system exposes design parameters (such as vector lane widths, memory hierarchy topology, and MLIR compiler passes) as structured schemas, bounding the agent's action space to permissible mutations verified by tool return codes. This machine-usable interface allows automated agents to query and mutate design state without bypassing the immutable audit trail inspected by human reviewers. Candidate generation must remain strictly decoupled from verification to expose genuine failure modes. As the Knight–Leveson multiversion independence experiment demonstrated in software systems, independent developers given the same specification frequently make identical cognitive errors [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. In an AI-native flow, if the same model drafts both the hardware accelerator netlist and its verification testbench, it replicates identical misinterpretations across both artifacts, producing false 100% pass rates on simulation that collapse upon physical tester bring-up. The design system must coordinate prediction, generation, and optimization against independent, multi-fidelity checks and explicit cost budgets, keeping every action anchored to the initial architecture question.

## Putting the Moonshot into Practice

Evaluating the Architecture 2.0 moonshot requires two independent tests, separating technical verification from organizational commitment. The first test evaluates whether the complete AI-native design system improved the architectural work against a credible conventional alternative run under matched budgets, tool access, and stopping conditions. A generated candidate demonstrates progress only when it improves the architecture result, reduces total engineering cost, or achieves both within its assessed envelope. The outcome can be positive (the candidate is superior), conservative (the reference baseline stands), or null (no candidate satisfies constraints); all three represent valid architecture results. Proving that an architectural concept is physically unroutable or thermally non-viable before an engineering organization invests millions in RTL implementation is a vital architectural finding, not a failed study.

The second test evaluates whether a named commitment authority within an accountable organization should commit capital to the design. This decision incorporates residual risk, physical limits, foundry tapeout schedules, and business trade-offs that no automated tool can resolve. The architect's technical recommendation informs this judgment without replacing it. Beyond individual studies, a broader program evaluation aggregates repeated studies across diverse design tasks and workloads. To claim program-level success, the AI-native design system must consistently improve architecture results or lower total costs across the declared scope. Based on public evidence in this edition, that program-level verdict remains open.

## Open Questions

Every chapter in this book ends the way it asks an architect to end a study, by naming what the argument rests on and did not establish. The questions here are the ones this chapter's case depends on and cannot settle. Later chapters, once they have taught an instrument, narrow to problems a reader could take into a lab.

- **Do the moves that changed computer architecture lie inside the design spaces we know how to search?** Every automated search starts from a space somebody wrote down, and all three layers described above are kinds of search. A cache sweep explores capacities. Nothing in a cache sweep proposes a cache. In physical and scientific domains, physics-informed methods succeed because immutable conservation laws constrain the hypothesis space, whereas unconstrained *tabula rasa* models waste compute rediscovering basic physical laws. Yet if automated systems are initialized only with human microarchitectural templates and classical design spaces, they can never discover radically discontinuous, non-intuitive operating points (such as systolic arrays or wafer-scale interconnects). Establishing how much architectural domain knowledge must be hardcoded as inductive bias versus how much should be discovered autonomously is the central open dilemma of architecture search.

- **How much of a finished design can a compact statement of intent actually determine?** A two-sentence product request was expanded here into eight requirement domains, and the expansion was treated as work an architect does rather than as something that might not terminate. Nobody has measured how much of a real chip a short statement of intent fixes. The reason an L2 cache is 2\ MiB rather than 4\ MiB usually lives in the head of whoever ran the study and leaves when they do, so two generations later the study runs again from scratch. Contract theory names that residue incomplete contracting and attaches an organizational consequence to it: the party that fills in what was never written holds real control whatever the specification document says. Whether that unwritten intent can be bounded by formal specification-coverage metrics, or inevitably leaves automated systems to make uninspected microarchitectural choices that tool defaults dictate, remains unmeasured.

- **Can an AI-native design system move the hardware–software boundary, or only optimize inside the one an architect drew?** Subsystem optimizers work because an architect fixes the interfaces, the objective, and the permitted moves before the search starts, which makes everything the optimizer does legal by construction. The layer above is defined by taking that away, and the definition assumes the requirement domains are coupled tightly enough for the difference to matter. If you add a custom vector instruction and no compiler emits it, there is nothing to execute and nothing to measure until months of software engineering work is completed. If those domains turn out to be loosely coupled, a coordinator over subsystem optimizers recovers most of the result and the larger apparatus is unnecessary.

- **When a machine produces the design, what did the architect contribute, and what would have to be on the record for anyone other than that architect to know it?** Commitment authority was declared nondelegable above, which presumes there is a contribution to be accountable for and that somebody could point at it. Patent offices have already been forced to rule on a version of this and ruled narrowly, that an inventor must be a person, which leaves somebody signing for a structure a search found and they had never seen. Photography settled the same problem in 1884, and the answer was that the work lives in the choices made before the machine acts, in the framing, the timing, and the decision that this one counts. A design carries thousands of such choices, made by a team, and almost none of them are written down. That much is testable now. Log every choice on a live project, then hand reviewers only the finished chip and see what they can recover.

- **How do you learn from a decision whose consequences arrive two years after you make it?** Everything described here is a loop, and a loop teaches you something only if the return arrives while you can still act on it. Eighteen to thirty months separate an architectural commitment from the first honest measurement of it, and by then the team has committed the next two products. Every faster stand-in the discipline uses was adopted because it was fast, not because anyone showed it predicts the slow one. Aviation met the same shape and answered it structurally, harvesting near misses because the real events were too rare to learn from, which worked only because reporting was confidential and unpunished. Neither half of that transfers directly. Nobody has published which pre-silicon signals predict post-silicon fidelity across product generations, and whether that gap can be closed through synthetic errata benchmarks on open tapeouts or through zero-knowledge surrogate calibration across closed programs remains unattempted.

## Summary

This opening chapter established the Architecture 2.0 moonshot around the industrial Lighthouse case study. A compact prompt is not a specification. It conceals eight coupled requirement domains spanning workloads, ABI contracts, compute organizations, memory hierarchies, power envelopes, compilers, physical constraints, and signoff checks. Before treating a request as an executable target, architects must define these underlying obligations, legal alternatives, physical limits, and acceptance checks.

Point AI assistance accelerates isolated tasks within established workflows (Layer 1) and subsystem optimizers tune local parameters within fixed containers (Layer 2), while a complete AI-native design system restructures the vertical stack around closed-loop search and multi-tool orchestration (Layer 3). The moonshot represents the program-level ambition that such a Layer 3 system can carry compact intent through to physically realizable silicon, an outcome this edition treats as an open question.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Explicit specification over compact intent.** A high-level prompt must expand into explicit workload traces, ABI contracts, memory hierarchies, physical constraints, and verification checks before any candidate can drive executable engineering.
- **Artifact qualification standard.** Syntactically valid code or successful local tool runs are merely candidate artifacts until qualified by rigorous measurements and checks under declared operating conditions.
- **Architecture result and design-system contribution measured apart.** Architecture 2.0 requires evaluating the architectural design quality against reference baselines separately from measuring the net productivity and engineering cost reductions of the AI-native design system itself.
- **Nondelegable commitment authority.** Automated generators and learned surrogates propose candidate designs, while a named human commitment authority retains nondelegable approval rights over silicon capital commitments and baseline specification updates.
:::

The Architecture 2.0 moonshot matters because modern computer architecture has hit structural complexity limits. @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales evaluates the compounding physical, software, and evaluation pressures behind those limits, and why they now exceed what conventional design practice can absorb.
